newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader sets up anti-kidnapping squad.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader sets up anti-kidnapping squad.

text.p: Chechen authorities plan to set up a special mobile investigative brigade, including judges of Islamic law, to tackle a wave of kidnappings sweeping their breakaway region, Itar-Tass news agency said on Monday.

It quoted Deputy Prosecutor General Magomed Magomadov as saying Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov had ordered the unit set up in a bid to end the many cases of hostage-taking after last week's abduction of two Britons.

The unit would group about 300 lawyers, detectives and judges, reporting directly to Maskhadov, Magomadov said. Judges will rule on kidnapping cases on the spot, in accordance with strict Sharia law. Maskhadov has said hostage-takers will face the death penalty.
Last week two British aid workers, Camilla Carr and Jon James, were seized from the house where they were staying by a group of armed, masked men.
On Sunday Maskhadov lambasted his top security officials over the incident and gave them 24 hours to come up with a plan to free the Britons and other hostages.
Police have detained and interrogated several people the two Britons had been working with, including their bodyguards, but have reported no progress so far.
Hostage-takers usually ask for money for the return of their captives but by Monday there had been no word of any demands for the release of the Britons.
Hostage-taking has become a huge problem in Chechnya, where Russian troops fought a bloody campaign against separatist forces for 21 months until last August.

The Britons had been working for the Centre for Peacemaking and Community Development, which is involved in the psychological rehabilitation of children affected by the conflict, in which tens of thousands of people died and many more were injured or made homeless.
Major international aid organisations withdrew most of their staff from the region after six Red Cross workers were shot dead in their beds in December by unknown gunmen.
Some foreigners are still working in Grozny for smaller aid organisations, but they keep a low profile.
On Monday the British aid agency Merlin said it had instructed its expatriate staff not to enter Grozny until further notice.
"But Grozny still desperately needs medicines and clean water, and we are determined to carry on distributing these through local staff," it said in a statement.
